issues.legal_issue: A certificate permitting an appeal must state adequate reasons, including the question of public or private importance to be determined, but a defective certificate need not be vacated when the appeal has no merit.
material_facts: The matter was an appeal brought under a certificate granted by the High Court.
The certificate did not set out the question of public or private importance that was to be determined in the appeal.
The Court found no merit in the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The certificate was defective because it lacked adequate reasons identifying the question of importance, but the Court did not vacate it because the appeal had no merit.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution, a High Court certificate must be supported by adequate reasons and must state the question of public or private importance that, in the High Court's opinion, falls to be determined in the appeal. The Court found it unnecessary to vacate the certificate in this case because the appeal lacked merit.

predicates.certified_appeal: The matter was an appeal brought under a certificate granted by a lower court.
predicates.certificate_omits_importance_question: The certificate did not state the question of public or private importance to be determined in the appeal.
predicates.appeal_lacks_merit: The Supreme Court concluded that the appeal had no merit.

issues.definition: When an appeal proceeds under a certificate that omits the question of importance and the appeal lacks merit, the certificate is treated as defective but is not vacated.

issues.legal_issue: Whether an agreement granting occupancy of immovable property creates a lease or a licence depends on the parties' intention, assessed from the agreement and surrounding circumstances; exclusive possession is significant but not conclusive.
material_facts: The written agreement described the arrangement as a leave and licence and stated that the occupant would have no tenancy rights, but those descriptions were not decisive of the parties' intention.
The occupant was given exclusive possession of a loft, and the grantor reserved neither possession of any part of it nor a right of entry.
The loft had a separate entrance used by the occupant's customers, and the occupant's stock remained there after business hours.
The parties were both cloth merchants, the occupant was permitted to use the loft for that business, and the only consideration was a monthly payment.
There was no evidence that the arrangement arose from sympathy, friendship, relationship, or a similar personal motive.
The written terms specified a one-year period, restricted use to cloth trading, prohibited transfer or subletting, and required a month's notice for termination.
issues.conclusion: The agreement created an interest in the loft and operated as a lease, not a licence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Easements Act defines a licence as a right to do something on another's immovable property that does not amount to an easement or an interest in that property. Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act defines a lease as a transfer of a right to enjoy immovable property. The controlling test is whether the agreement, read in light of surrounding circumstances, was intended to create an interest in the property; the parties' labels are evidence but are not decisive. Exclusive possession is significant but not conclusive. The Court relied on Mrs. M. N. Clubwala v. Fida Hussain Saheb, [1964] 6 S.C.R. 642.

rule.if: occupancy_classification_case and exclusive_possession_granted and grantor_reserved_no_possession_or_entry and occupant_has_independent_access_and_use and payment_is_the_only_consideration and circumstances_indicate_property_interest

predicates.occupancy_classification_case: The dispute requires a court to determine whether an agreement for occupancy of immovable property creates a lease or a licence.
predicates.exclusive_possession_granted: The grantor placed the occupant in exclusive possession of the premises.
predicates.grantor_reserved_no_possession_or_entry: The grantor reserved neither possession of part of the premises nor a right of entry into them.
predicates.occupant_has_independent_access_and_use: The premises had separate access used by the occupant's customers, and the occupant kept business stock there after business hours.
predicates.payment_is_the_only_consideration: The occupant's payment was the only consideration for the arrangement, without evidence of a personal or relational motive for granting occupancy.
predicates.circumstances_indicate_property_interest: The agreement's terms and surrounding circumstances, considered together, indicated that the parties intended to create an interest in the premises despite describing the arrangement as a licence and disclaiming tenancy rights.

issues.definition: When an occupancy-classification dispute involves exclusive possession, no reserved possession or entry, independent use, payment as the only consideration, and circumstances indicating an intended property interest, the agreement operates as a lease.
